title: AI agents are paying invoices now. Finance needs new rules
body_markdown:
# A bot just paid an invoice. Finance has a new kind of cardholder


An AI agent paid a real supplier invoice last month.


It entered the supplier's portal, authenticated itself, used a payment credential connected to an approved invoice and completed the payment. Nobody had to copy card details into the browser or press the final button.


The payment was part of a live pilot involving Visa, BILL and Billtrust, and it is already processing transactions between participating buyers and suppliers.


At first, this sounds like another small piece of payment automation. Then you picture it happening inside a finance department.


Most automated payment processes still end with a person. The software reads the invoice, matches it, prepares the payment and sends someone a notification. A human logs in and releases the money.


This time, the software finished the job itself.


### **Software now has a way to pay**


The payment networks have been preparing for this.


On July 2nd 2026, Visa announced that AI agents had completed live purchases with merchants in Europe. The agents searched for products, selected what to buy and initiated payments based on instructions from cardholders.


Mastercard has gone a step further with Agent Pay for Machines, a service designed for payments that happen automatically between systems.


One of Mastercard's examples involves a logistics agent managing a delivery. As the shipment moves, the agent could pay for freight, reserve a loading bay, buy temporary monitoring data and settle warehouse fees.


That is where this becomes more interesting than an AI shopping assistant.


A person might ask an agent to book one hotel. A business could have agents making thousands of small purchases throughout the day, with many of those transactions happening too quickly for anyone to review individually.


### **Developers can now give an agent the payment step**


Stripe has made this as small as a single command.


Its new[stripe pay plugin](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/pay) for the Stripe CLI lets software send money to another business using that business's Stripe profile handle. Developers already build and test agents in the command line, so a payment can now be one more instruction an agent runs.


Stripe clearly expects agents to use it. The command has an --agent option that returns the transfer details in a format software can read, instead of a screen designed for a person.


The documentation also reads a bit like a finance policy. If the recipient isn't clear, the agent is told to search Stripe's directory, asking the user to choose without guessing. The flag that actually sends the money should only be added after the user confirms the recipient, amount, currency and the account the money comes from. There is also a dry-run mode that tests the whole flow without moving anything.


For now it's a preview for eligible businesses in the US and UK. Transfers work in USD, GBP and USDC, from a funded Stripe Treasury account. A finance team in Dubai can't switch it on tomorrow.


The direction is still clear, though. A payments company now offers a payment as something an agent can run on its own, and the approval rules are written into the instructions.


### **Corporate spending was designed around people**


Think about how a corporate card works today.


The card belongs to an employee, who belongs to a department and reports to a manager. Finance gives them a limit, blocks certain types of merchants and can ask them about an unusual transaction.


If the employee leaves, the card is cancelled.


An AI agent does not fit into that setup very neatly. It may have been built by the technology team, deployed by operations and funded from a marketing budget. Several versions of it could be running at the same time, and each version might use other agents to complete part of its work.


Putting all of that spending on an employee's card would make the audit trail almost useless. The statement would show the employee's name even though the employee did not choose the supplier, timing or amount.


Visa and Mastercard are therefore working on separate identities for agents. The idea is that a merchant or bank should be able to recognise which agent is making the purchase and confirm that it has permission to do so.


The industry has even found a name for this: Know Your Agent.


We spent years building Know Your Customer checks. Now apparently the bots need onboarding too.


### **Who approved the payment?**


Identifying the agent only answers part of the question.


Imagine asking an AI travel agent to organise a three-day sales trip for less than AED 8,000. The agent books a flight, hotel and airport transfer, and the total comes to AED 7,600.


Everything looks fine until finance notices that the hotel cost more than the company's normal nightly limit. The agent stayed within the overall trip budget because every cheaper hotel near the meeting was full.


Did it follow the policy?


A person could write an expense note explaining what happened. An agent may have compared hundreds of options and made the decision through several model calls that nobody watched.


Finance will probably want more context than the agent's name. The useful record would include the instruction it received, the budget it was given and the policy that applied when the payment happened.


Visa's supplier-payment pilot works in a similar way. The agent uses controls connected to an approved payment instruction and a specific invoice, so it cannot simply enter the portal and choose something else to pay.


This may be what approval starts to look like when agents spend company money.


### **The budget becomes the biggest part of the permission**


Companies will struggle to use agents if a person has to approve every transaction they make.


Imagine an agent that buys cloud capacity whenever demand increases. If it has to wait for the finance team each time, customers may already be gone by the time someone approves the extra capacity.


Giving the agent unlimited access would obviously create another problem.


A more realistic arrangement is to approve the boundaries in advance. The agent could receive AED 20,000 each month, an approved list of suppliers and rules about what it is allowed to purchase. Inside those limits, it could act without asking for permission each time.


This is already how corporate cards work in a simpler form. Employees receive a limit and a set of controls, then make decisions inside them.


The difference is speed. An employee might make ten purchases in a week, while an agent could make ten thousand.


Mastercard expects some machine payments to be worth only fractions of a cent. An agent might buy a few seconds of computing power, one piece of live data or access to a specialist model for a single task.


No employee would spend twenty minutes arranging a payment worth three fils. Software does not mind.


### **The receipt will matter less**


When finance reviews a normal expense, the receipt explains what was purchased. If the reason is unclear, someone can ask the employee.


That becomes harder when an agent makes the decision.


A receipt may show that software purchased additional data at 2:14 am, although it will not explain that the agent needed the data to complete a customer request before a deadline.


The audit trail may need to preserve the reason for the transaction as well as the transaction itself. Finance will want to see which agent spent the money, who authorised it and what the agent was trying to achieve.


Nobody will want a 40,000-line record of everything the model processed. The explanation needs to be short enough for a person to understand.


Something like: "Purchased additional delivery data for Order 4832 because the original provider was unavailable. Cost remained within the approved limit."


If agents can produce that context reliably, they may end up writing better expense notes than many employees.


### **Finance will design the boundaries**


In a recent speech about AI agents and payments, Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller described agentic commerce as an early development that could significantly reshape payments if it grows.


The technology is early, but the direction is becoming easier to see.


Agents are moving from recommending purchases to completing them. Payment networks are giving them identities, credentials and spending limits. Finance systems will eventually need to recognise software as a real participant in company spending.


This gives finance a different kind of job.


Someone has to decide how much money the agent can access, which suppliers it can use and what evidence it must leave behind. Someone also has to decide when a payment needs a person and when the agent can handle it alone.


The next corporate cardholder may never travel, lose a receipt or forget to submit an expense.


It may also make more purchases in one afternoon than the rest of the company makes in a month.


When that happens, asking who made the payment will be the easy part.


The interesting question will be what we gave the agent permission to do.
